items.example_en: Hello, my name is Maria.
items.note: The first в is silent. The default greeting to anyone you address as вы.

items.example_en: Hi! How are things?
items.note: Only for friends, family, and children.

items.example_en: Good morning, have you had breakfast?
items.note: добрый день and добрый вечер follow through the day.

items.example_en: How are things? Fine, thanks.
items.note: нормально is the standard neutral answer, not lukewarm as in English.

items.example_en: Excuse me, what is your name?
items.note: Literally how do they call you. Informal: как тебя зовут?

items.example_en: Very nice to meet you, I'm Pavel.
items.note: Literally very pleasant.

items.example_en: One coffee, please.
items.note: Does double duty as please and as you're welcome.

items.example_en: Thank you very much for the help.
Excuse me, where is the station?
items.note: Informal извини. Use it before asking a stranger anything.

items.example_en: Sorry, I didn't catch that.
items.note: Slightly weightier than извините.

items.example_en: Sorry! No problem.
items.note: Literally nothing terrible. In ничего, the г sounds like v.

items.example_en: Would you be so kind as to repeat that.
items.note: The politest way to open a request to a stranger.

items.example_en: Goodbye, see you tomorrow!
items.note: Literally until the meeting.

items.example_en: All right, bye!
items.note: Also means for now or while, depending on context.

items.example_en: Sorry, I don't understand.
items.note: The single most useful sentence of your first week.

items.example_en: Please speak more slowly.
items.note: The comparative ending -ее does the work of English more.

items.english: how do you say ... in Russian?
items.example_en: How do you say window in Russian?
items.note: по-русски is an adverb: in the Russian way.

items.example_en: Sorry, I speak Russian badly.
items.note: Said early, it makes everyone slow down for you.

items.example_en: My name is Stijn, and yours?
items.note: Literally they call me. меня is accusative.

items.example: Я из Бельгии, но живу в Москве.
items.example_en: I'm from Belgium, but I live in Moscow.
items.note: из takes the genitive: Бельгия becomes Бельгии.

items.example: Я живу в Санкт-Петербурге уже три года.
items.example_en: I've been living in Saint Petersburg for three years.
items.note: в plus prepositional for location: в Москве, в городе.

items.example: Мне тридцать лет, а брату двадцать восемь.
items.example_en: I'm thirty, and my brother is twenty-eight.
items.note: Dative plus лет: literally to me are thirty years. 1 год, 2-4 года, 5+ лет.

items.example_en: I have a sister.
items.note: Russian has no verb to have: literally by me there is.

items.example_en: I've been married for ten years.
items.note: A woman says я замужем. The two words are completely different.

items.example_en: I work at a school.
items.note: Regular first-conjugation verb.

items.example_en: I'm a student, I study biology.
items.note: No verb to be in the present tense, and no article. Female: студентка.

items.english: what do you do for a living?
items.example_en: And what do you do for a living?
items.note: Instrumental case: literally as whom do you work.

items.example: Я изучаю русский язык шесть месяцев.
items.example_en: I've been studying Russian for six months.
items.note: изучать is deliberate study; учиться is being a student somewhere.

items.example_en: I speak a little Russian.
Excuse me, do you speak English?
items.note: Word order stays the same; intonation makes it a question.

items.example_en: Three coffees, please.
items.note: один agrees in gender: один стол, одна книга, одно окно.

items.example_en: That'll be ten roubles.
items.note: After 5 and above, the counted noun goes into the genitive plural.

items.example_en: The bus is coming in twenty minutes.
items.note: через plus accusative means in, after an interval.

items.example_en: The ticket costs a hundred roubles.
That cost one and a half thousand.
items.note: Feminine noun, so it declines like one: тысячи, тысяче.

items.example_en: How much does this bag cost?
items.note: сколько always takes the genitive: сколько времени, сколько денег.

items.example_en: Excuse me, what time is it?
items.note: Colloquially: сколько времени?

items.example_en: It's eight in the morning.
items.note: час after 1, часа after 2-4, часов after 5 and up.

items.example_en: The train leaves at half past eight.
items.note: Literally half of the ninth hour, so it means 8:30, not 9:30.

items.example_en: In the morning I run in the park.
items.note: Instrumental case as an adverb: днём, вечером, ночью.

items.example_en: The weather is good today.
items.note: The д is pronounced as v, like in ничего.

items.example_en: I'm busy right now, I'll call back.
items.note: Often reduced to something like щас in fast speech.

items.example_en: See you on Monday.
items.note: в plus accusative for days. Days are lowercase.

items.example_en: What are you doing at the weekend?
items.note: A plural adjective used as a noun: literally the days off.

items.example_en: My birthday is in January.
items.note: в plus prepositional for months, and the stress shifts: январь becomes январе.

items.example_en: We'll discuss it next week.
items.note: Weeks take на, not в: на этой неделе, на прошлой неделе.

items.example_en: The shops are closed on the first of May.
items.note: Neuter ordinal plus genitive month. On that date: первого мая.

items.example_en: I always have breakfast at home.
items.note: Family: иногда, часто, редко, никогда.
